body:
What is sound?

Sound is a form of energy produced by vibrating objects. It travels from a source to a listener through a material medium and can produce the sensation of hearing.

When a metal bell is struck, its surface moves rapidly back and forth. This movement is called a vibration. The vibrating bell disturbs the surrounding air, allowing sound to reach a listener.

Vibration: The repeated to-and-fro motion of an object about its normal or equilibrium position.

How sound is produced

Every ordinary sound has a vibrating source. Different objects produce sound because different parts of them vibrate.

Sound sourceVibrating part
Metal bellMetal body of the bell
Tabla or dholakStretched membrane
Sitar or guitarStretched strings
FluteAir column inside the instrument
Human voiceVocal cords in the larynx

In human beings, air from the lungs passes through the larynx, or voice box, causing the vocal cords to vibrate. The resulting sound is modified by the mouth and other parts of the vocal passage to produce speech.

How sound travels through a medium

The movement of sound from its source to another place is called propagation of sound. The substance through which sound travels is called a medium.

When an object vibrates, it disturbs nearby particles of the medium. These particles transfer the disturbance to neighbouring particles. The process continues, carrying sound energy away from the source.

The particles of the medium do not travel from the source to the listener. Instead, they vibrate around their usual positions while the disturbance travels through the medium.

Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases

  • Gases: Ordinary conversation takes place because sound travels through air.
  • Liquids: Sound travels through water, allowing underwater communication and echo detection.
  • Solids: Sound can travel through materials such as wood, steel and tightly stretched strings.

The nature of the medium affects the speed at which sound travels. However, a material medium is necessary in every case.

Why sound cannot travel through a vacuum

Sound is a mechanical wave because it requires particles of a material medium to carry the disturbance. A vacuum contains no material medium through which ordinary sound can propagate.

Consider an electric bell inside a sealed glass jar. As air is gradually removed, the sound heard outside becomes weaker even though the bell continues vibrating. This demonstrates the importance of a material medium.

Consequently, astronauts cannot communicate directly by shouting across the vacuum of space. Radio communication is possible because radio waves are electromagnetic waves and do not require a material medium.

Sound and light are different: Sound requires a material medium. Light can travel through a vacuum.

Prelims focus

  • Sound is produced by vibrating objects.
  • Sound is a mechanical wave and carries energy.
  • Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases.
  • Sound cannot propagate through a vacuum.
  • Human speech originates from vibrations of the vocal cords.
  • Trap: The disturbance travels through the medium; its particles do not travel all the way from the source to the listener.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 13, Sound, sections 13.1–13.3; GCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 10, Sound, sections 10.1–10.3; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 12, Sound, sections 12.1–12.2.1.]

pictures.caption: A vibrating bell produces sound that travels through the surrounding air.

title: Production and Propagation of Sound

body:
Sound travels through air as a longitudinal wave

When a vibrating object produces sound in air, it creates alternating regions of increased and decreased air pressure. These pressure variations move away from the source as a wave.

Ordinary sound in air is a longitudinal wave. In a longitudinal wave, particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction in which the wave travels.

Longitudinal wave: A wave in which the particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of propagation of the disturbance.

Formation of compressions and rarefactions

Consider a vibrating object moving forward and backward in air.

  • When the object moves forward, it pushes nearby air particles closer together, producing a region of higher pressure and density called a compression.
  • When the object moves backward, the nearby particles become more widely separated, producing a region of lower pressure and density called a rarefaction.

Continuous vibration produces successive compressions and rarefactions. These regions travel through the medium and constitute the sound wave.

Compression and rarefaction

PropertyCompressionRarefaction
Particle arrangementParticles closer togetherParticles farther apart
PressureHigher than averageLower than average
DensityHigher than averageLower than average
Pressure graphPeakValley

A graph showing the pressure variations of a sound wave is often drawn as a smooth curve with peaks and valleys. This curve represents pressure or density variations; it does not mean that air particles physically move up and down in that curved pattern.

Longitudinal waves and transverse waves

Mechanical waves can also be classified according to the direction in which particles vibrate relative to the travelling disturbance.

FeatureLongitudinal waveTransverse wave
Particle vibrationParallel to wave propagationPerpendicular to wave propagation
Characteristic patternCompressions and rarefactionsCrests and troughs
School-level exampleSound travelling through airWave on a stretched rope

A stretched spring provides a useful example of a longitudinal wave. When one end is pushed and pulled along the length of the spring, closely spaced and widely spaced coils travel along it. Individual coils move back and forth about their original positions.

In contrast, when one end of a stretched rope is moved up and down, the disturbance travels along the rope while its particles move perpendicular to that direction.

Wavelength of a sound wave

The wavelength is the distance between 2 consecutive points of a wave that are in the same stage of vibration.

For a longitudinal sound wave, it is the distance between 2 successive compressions or between 2 successive rarefactions.

Wavelength is represented by the Greek letter λ (lambda). Its SI unit is the metre (m).

The distance from a compression to the next rarefaction is only half a wavelength. A complete wavelength extends from one compression to the next compression, or from one rarefaction to the next rarefaction.

Prelims focus

  • Ordinary sound waves in air are longitudinal waves.
  • In a longitudinal wave, particle vibration is parallel to wave propagation.
  • Compression corresponds to higher pressure and density.
  • Rarefaction corresponds to lower pressure and density.
  • Wavelength is represented by λ and measured in metres.
  • Trap: A curved pressure-wave graph does not show air particles moving transversely.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 12, Sound, sections 12.2–12.2.3; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, Sound, sections 11.2–11.2.2.]

pictures.alt: A vibrating source sends alternating compressions and rarefactions through air; particles vibrate parallel to travel, and wavelength joins consecutive matching regions.
pictures.caption: Sound propagates through air as alternating compressions and rarefactions.

pictures.alt: Sound particles vibrate parallel to wave travel; rope particles vibrate perpendicular to it. Both oscillate about equilibrium positions.
pictures.caption: Longitudinal and transverse waves differ in the direction of particle vibration.

title: Longitudinal Sound Waves, Compressions and Rarefactions

body:
Frequency: Number of vibrations per second

The frequency of a periodic vibration is the number of complete oscillations occurring in 1 second. The frequency of a sound wave is also the number of complete wave cycles passing a fixed point each second.

Frequency is commonly represented by f and is measured in hertz (Hz).

A frequency of 100 Hz means that 100 complete vibrations occur in 1 second. A frequency of 200 Hz means that 200 complete vibrations occur in the same interval.

The unit hertz is named after the physicist Heinrich Rudolf Hertz.

Frequency and pitch

Pitch is the characteristic of sound that enables us to distinguish a high or shrill sound from a low or deep sound. Pitch depends primarily on frequency.

  • Higher frequency produces higher pitch.
  • Lower frequency produces lower pitch.

For example, a whistle generally produces a higher-pitched sound than a large drum because its characteristic vibrations have a higher frequency.

A louder sound is not necessarily a higher-pitched sound. A deep drumbeat may be very loud while a high-pitched whistle may be relatively soft.

Time period: Duration of 1 oscillation

The time period is the time required to complete 1 oscillation or vibration. It is represented by T and measured in seconds (s).

Frequency and time period are reciprocal quantities:

\(f = \frac{1}{T}\)

\(T = \frac{1}{f}\)

Frequency and time period

If an object performs 100 complete vibrations in 1 second, its frequency is 100 Hz.

Its time period is \(T = 1/100 = 0.01\) s.

If the frequency increases, the time taken for each vibration decreases.

Amplitude: Maximum displacement from equilibrium

The amplitude of a vibrating object is its maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.

In a sound wave, amplitude can also describe the maximum variation in pressure or density from its average value.

A larger vibration generally produces a sound wave with greater amplitude and energy. Under comparable listening conditions, a wave with greater amplitude is normally heard as louder.

Amplitude and loudness

Loudness is the perceived strength of a sound. It depends strongly on sound amplitude, but also on factors such as distance from the source and the sensitivity of human hearing.

When a table is struck gently, its vibrations generally have smaller amplitude and produce a softer sound. When it is struck harder, the amplitude is usually greater and the sound is louder.

Sound intensity is a physical measure of sound energy passing per second through a unit area. Loudness is the corresponding auditory sensation and is not identical to intensity.

Speed, frequency and wavelength

The speed of sound is the distance travelled by a sound disturbance in 1 second. Its SI unit is metres per second (m/s).

During 1 complete oscillation, a periodic sound wave travels a distance equal to 1 wavelength.

The relationship between speed, frequency and wavelength is:

\(v = f\lambda\)

Here, v is wave speed, f is frequency and λ is wavelength.

Finding the wavelength

Suppose a sound travels at 340 m/s and has a frequency of 200 Hz.

\(\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{340}{200} = 1.7\,\mathrm{m}\)

The wavelength is 1.7 m.

Under the same conditions in the same medium, the speed of ordinary sound is nearly independent of frequency. Therefore, if frequency increases while speed remains constant, wavelength decreases.

Quality of sound

Different musical instruments can produce sounds with the same pitch and similar loudness, yet they may still sound different. This distinguishing characteristic is called quality or timbre.

Thus, pitch, loudness and quality describe different aspects of sound. Frequency is primarily associated with pitch, amplitude with loudness, and the combination of frequency components with timbre.

Prelims focus

  • Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz).
  • Time period is measured in seconds (s).
  • Frequency and time period satisfy \(f = 1/T\).
  • Higher frequency generally means higher pitch.
  • Greater amplitude generally means greater loudness under comparable conditions.
  • Wave speed, frequency and wavelength satisfy \(v = f\lambda\).
  • Trap: Increasing frequency does not necessarily increase the speed of sound in the same medium.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 12, Sound, section 12.2.3, printed pages 163–166; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 13, Sound, section 13.5; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 13, Motion and Time, section 13.3; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, Sound, section 11.2.2.]

pictures.alt: Equal-amplitude waves at 100 Hz and 200 Hz differ in pitch; equal-frequency waves with amplitudes A and 2A differ in loudness.
pictures.caption: Frequency primarily determines pitch, while amplitude strongly influences loudness.

title: Frequency, Amplitude, Pitch, Loudness and Wave Speed

body:
What determines the speed of sound?

Sound does not travel instantaneously. It requires a finite time to move from one place to another.

The speed of sound depends mainly on the properties of the medium and its physical conditions, especially temperature.

Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases, but it does not travel at the same speed in all substances.

Comparing sound speeds in different substances

The following textbook values illustrate the substantial differences in sound speed among selected materials at 25°C.

MediumSubstanceSpeed at 25°C (m/s)
GasAir346
LiquidSeawater1531
SolidSteel5960

In these examples, sound travels fastest through steel and slowest through air. The general school-level comparison is that sound often travels faster through solids than liquids, and faster through liquids than gases. Exact speed, however, depends on the particular material and its physical conditions.

It would be incorrect to conclude that every solid must transmit sound faster than every liquid under all conditions.

Effect of temperature

The speed of sound in air increases as its temperature increases.

For example, standard textbook values give approximately:

  • 331 m/s in air at 0°C.
  • 344 m/s in air at 22°C.

When solving a numerical problem, use the temperature and sound speed supplied in the question rather than assuming that a single value applies everywhere.

The speed of sound through seawater also depends on its physical conditions. Temperature, pressure and salinity can affect the speed.

Why lightning is seen before thunder is heard

Lightning produces both light and sound. The light travels much faster than sound, so the flash reaches an observer before the sound of thunder.

For a simple illustration, if lightning occurs about 1 km away and the speed of sound in air is taken as 340 m/s, the sound takes approximately 3 seconds to reach the observer. The travel time of the light over this distance is negligible in comparison.

Frequency does not determine sound speed in a fixed medium

A low-pitched sound and a high-pitched sound can travel through the same air at almost the same speed when the physical conditions are identical.

Their frequencies and wavelengths may differ, but the speed of propagation is determined mainly by the medium.

Do not confuse speed with loudness or pitch. A loud or shrill sound does not automatically travel faster than a soft or low-pitched sound.

Prelims focus

  • Sound travels at a finite speed.
  • At 25°C, the textbook values are 346 m/s in air, 1531 m/s in seawater and 5960 m/s in steel.
  • The speed of sound in air increases with temperature.
  • Thunder is heard after lightning is seen because light travels much faster than sound.
  • The speed of ordinary sound is nearly independent of frequency in the same medium under fixed conditions.
  • Trap: Greater frequency does not necessarily mean greater sound speed.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 12, Sound, sections 12.2.3–12.2.4 and Table 12.1, printed pages 165–167; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, Sound, section 11.2.3 and Table 11.1; NOAA National Ocean Service, How far does sound travel in the ocean?, updated 23 September 2026, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Light and thunder start together about 1 km away; light arrives first, while sound at about 340 m/s takes about 3 seconds.
pictures.caption: Lightning and thunder originate together, but light reaches the observer much earlier.

title: Speed of Sound in Different Media
